title: Revealed: Expensive gas behind ‘nearly 90%’ of rise in UK electricity bills - Carbon Brief
gist: Nesta analysis shared with Carbon Brief finds wholesale gas costs explain about 90% (£161 of £180) of the real-terms rise in UK household electricity bills since 2020 and 81% of the rise in dual-fuel bills, contradicting the claim that net-zero drives bills. With UK wholesale gas at 220p/therm on 19 October, above the 2022 average, bills are expected to jump sharply under the January 2027 cap.

themes.theme: Gas as driver of UK electricity bills

insights.claim: Wholesale costs driven by expensive gas account for about 90% (£161) of the £180 real-terms rise in typical UK annual household electricity bills between Q4 2020 and Q4 2026, per Nesta analysis.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Retail power-price risk in the UK tracks the gas price, so gas moves are the lead indicator for bill and political pressure.
insights.quote: Some 90% of this increase (£161) is due to wholesale costs, driven by the price of gas.
insights.locator: The figure below shows that, after accounting for inflation

insights.claim: UK wholesale gas stood at 220p per therm (£75/MWh) on 19 October 2026, above the 2022 average of 210p/therm, the highest level since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Gas is back above 2022 crisis-average levels, a stress marker for UK energy-intensive sectors and household budgets.
insights.locator: Now, amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East

insights.claim: Wholesale gas costs explain 77% (£283) of the £368 real-terms rise in household gas bills since 2020.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Gas-bill inflation is overwhelmingly a commodity story, not a policy-cost story.
insights.locator: Since 2020, household gas bills have increased

insights.claim: Real-terms dual-fuel bills for a typical UK household rose 47%, from £1,175 per year in October 2020 to £1,723 in October 2026, and wholesale costs account for £444 (81%) of that increase.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Quantifies the household squeeze that drives budget and cost-of-living politics.
insights.locator: After accounting for inflation, total dual-fuel bills

insights.claim: Britain is particularly exposed to gas prices because over 80% of households are connected to gas mains and the electricity system still relies too much on gas as the marginal unit.
insights.speaker: Andrew Sissons
insights.so_what: Marginal-unit pricing means gas sets power prices even when most generation is cleaner; reducing gas on the margin is the structural fix.

insights.claim: The Nesta analysis contradicts the idea embedded in UK media and politics that the net-zero target is to blame for high energy bills.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Evidence against the anti-net-zero bills narrative matters for UK policy and budget risk around clean-energy support.
insights.locator: The analysis firmly contradicts the idea

insights.claim: Renewable contracts for difference are reducing electricity bills by £17 under the current price cap, while government has cut policy costs by moving 75% of legacy renewable support onto general taxation, ending the ECO scheme and temporarily removing VAT.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Policy costs are shrinking as a bill component, shifting burden to taxpayers, which matters for fiscal planning.

insights.claim: Government social and climate policy costs fell from £183 (16%) of typical dual-fuel bills in October 2020 to £114 (7%) under the October 2026 price cap.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: The policy-cost share of bills has halved, undercutting claims that levies are the cause of the rise.
insights.locator: In total, the cost of government social and climate policies

insights.claim: Electricity bills have begun to decouple from gas bills since the start of the Iran war, thanks to more UK renewable power and contracts for difference, so household electricity prices have risen far less than gas bills since the Hormuz crisis.
insights.speaker: Andrew Sissons
insights.so_what: Evidence that renewables dampen gas pass-through supports the case for faster electrification as a hedge against gas shocks.
insights.locator: Notably, household electricity prices have increased far less

insights.claim: Network costs have added £72 to typical UK electricity bills since 2020, mostly (£46) for transmission investment, with only £21 relating to balancing including constraint payments for turning off windfarms and turning on gas plants.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Grid build-out is the real, growing cost line; it is small next to gas but is the structural cost of electrification.
insights.locator: Network costs have added £72 to typical bills

insights.claim: Balancing costs in total make up just £35 (4%) of a typical £858 annual household electricity bill, even though wind constraint payments regularly receive extensive news coverage.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Headline constraint-payment stories overstate their share of bills, relevant to grid-reform and wind-curtailment sentiment.
insights.locator: Wind constraint payments regularly receive extensive news coverage

insights.claim: Wholesale costs make up the largest share of the current price cap at £757 (44%), followed by network costs at £417 (24%) and operating costs at £291 (17%); the £127 real-terms rise in network costs includes £72 for electricity and £55 for the gas grid.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Shows where the cap's cost stack sits; wholesale is the swing factor and networks the second lever.
insights.locator: Wholesale costs make up the largest share of the current cap

insights.claim: Upgrading the grid is not cost-neutral, but according to Nesta the price tag is dwarfed by the impact of rising gas prices; the Energy Networks Association says up to 80% of electricity grid investment is needed to maintain existing assets.
insights.speaker: Andrew Sissons
insights.so_what: Grid capex is largely replacement rather than net-zero expansion, tempering the claim that decarbonisation drives network costs.
insights.quote: Upgrading the grid is not cost-neutral, but that price tag is dwarfed by the impact of rising gas prices.

insights.claim: Energy supplier operating costs have risen £46 since 2020, thought to be driven by the cost of rising household energy debt, with supplier profits capped at 2.5% of bills.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Rising consumer arrears are showing up as a cost embedded in bills.
insights.locator: The Nesta figures show energy supplier operating costs

insights.claim: The UK government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea despite stating that it would not affect prices.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: North Sea supply approvals do not address price exposure, a point in the UK domestic gas-versus-electrification debate.
insights.locator: The analysis comes after the UK government gave its approval

insights.claim: Nesta argues the path to shielding UK households from global gas turmoil is clean electricity, electric vehicles and heat pumps, with growing electricity demand spreading grid upgrade costs more widely.
insights.speaker: Andrew Sissons
insights.so_what: Supports demand growth for electrification technologies in the UK as a policy direction.

insights.claim: Bills are expected to rise sharply under the January 2027 price cap, potentially by as much as a quarter, and the chancellor may take steps to help households and businesses at the 28 October budget.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Watch the 28 October budget and the January cap announcement for fiscal support and demand effects.
insights.locator: Media reports suggest the chancellor may take steps
